At appraisal, in 2018, Lao PDR had sustained rapid economic growth, averaging 7.8 percent annually over the preceding decade and ranked among the fastest-growing economies globally.

Growth was driven by natural resource exploitation and deeper regional integration under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), with services— particularly retail, tourism, and transport—playing an increasingly important role. Yet, this trajectory came with mounting challenges. Public debt had risen sharply, fueled in part by large-scale infrastructure investments, particularly in hydropower generation, and the Government of Lao PDR (GoL) had begun fiscal consolidation efforts, including expanding the tax base and strengthening tax administration. Further reforms were needed to enhance public investment management and address debt vulnerabilities. 2. Progress in poverty reduction was evident with absolute poverty declining from 24.6 percent in 2012 to 18.3 percent in 2018. A significant share of the population remained dependent on agriculture and highly vulnerable to shocks. Inequality persisted, reflected in a Gini index of 38.8 in 2018, while access to basic infrastructure and services, including transport—remained limited for the bottom 40 percent of the population. 3. Lao PDR’s exposure to climate and disaster risks compounded these challenges. Lao PDR is highly vulnerable to climate change due to its tropical climate, topography, and substantial poverty. Historical data showed annual expected losses from climatic events equivalent to 3–4 percent of GDP, with fiscal costs approaching 2 percent of government expenditures.

Major floods in 2013 and the 2015–16 El Niño event underscored the fragility of infrastructure, while climate projections indicated rising temperatures and more frequent extreme events, posing additional threats to economic activity and transport assets. Lao PDR ranks 142 out of 181 countries in the 2020 Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (GAIN Index), and its road infrastructure is especially at risk from climate-related events such as washouts and erosion during the rainy season. 4. Within the transport sector, the GoL prioritized large-scale infrastructure development to strengthen regional connectivity under its vision of transforming Lao PDR from landlocked to land-linked. While funding for the road sector rose to US$107 million in FY2017, allocations remained heavily skewed toward new construction and emergency repairs, contributing to rising public debt. Emergency repairs alone accounted for nearly 30 percent of the annual maintenance budget, reflecting both the impact of climate-related events and the pressing need for more resilient infrastructure. 5. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MPWT), responsible for the national road network, struggled to secure adequate and predictable financing for long-term maintenance.

The Road Fund—financed mainly through a fuel levy—expanded from US$2 million in 2002 to over US$80 million in 2016, yet its effectiveness was constrained by competing demands, weak prioritization mechanisms, and lengthy administrative procedures for budgeting, procurement, and contract management. These inefficiencies limited the adoption of a life-cycle management approach, resulting in chronic underfunding and neglected maintenance of the road network. 6. Road safety and overloading were significant concerns. Reported fatalities more than doubled between 2000 and 2010, reaching over 1,000 deaths in 2014, with motorcyclists disproportionately affected. Lao PDR recorded some of the highest GDP losses from road crashes in the region, driven by inadequate safety infrastructure, limited enforcement, and poor compliance with traffic rules. Large numbers of vehicle operators were unlicensed. Additionally, while the ASEAN standard was 11-tonne axle loads, most main roads in Lao PDR, including National Road 13 (NR13) North, were designed and built for an 8.2-tonne standard axle loads and were therefore vulnerable to damage from regional traffic. 7. At appraisal, in May 2018, improving the reliability and resilience of NR13 North was among the Ministry of Public Works and Transport’s (MPWT) key priorities.

NR13 North links the capital, Vientiane, to ten northern provinces and the Official Use Only Page 1 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT border with China, was the most heavily trafficked road in the country, and is critical to the Laotian economy, serving an important role in national and regional freight movements. Sections of NR13 North were approaching full capacity due to strong economic growth, trade expansion, and rapid growth in vehicle ownership. The road was in poor condition, with extensive pavement distress, insufficient drainage, inadequate safety features, and traffic bottlenecks particularly from Sikhai to Sikeut. Many stretches regularly flooded, disrupting traffic flow and resulting in pavement damage. 8. MPWT initially sought to reconstruct 58 km of NR13 North to a climate resilient standard under a ten-year toll road contract. Tolling met MPWT’s key objectives of ensuring efficient long-term maintenance and managing public investment costs. Although the most urbanized section from Sikhai to Sikeut was omitted from the toll proposal for socioeconomic reasons and would be improved with public financing,1 tolling was eventually rejected due to the lack of an alternative (non-tolled) route. 9. To address MPWT’s strategic priorities, an Output-and Performance-Based Road Contract (OPBRC) approach was adopted as an alternative to tolling.

OPBRC transfers construction and maintenance risks to the contractor which is paid for most – but not all – rehabilitation and improvement costs during a rehabilitation phase. Payment of the remainder is made contingent upon independent verification that contractually defined level of service standards are met over a longterm maintenance period. This model satisfied MPWT’s priorities of operationalizing a life-cycle asset management approach by creating incentives for contractors to deliver efficient and high-quality construction and preventive maintenance. OPBRC also strengthened fiscal discipline by enabling the Government to shift from short-term, ad-hoc budgeting to a multi-year, performance-driven maintenance regime with predictable costs. 10. The proposed investment in NR13 North was closely aligned with World Bank Group’s Country Partnership Framework (CPF) for Lao PDR (2017–2021). Rehabilitation and improvement of NR13 North directly supported Focus Area 1, particularly Objective 1.3: Investing in infrastructure for growth and inclusion, by improving access to all-weather roads, reducing travel time for rural populations, and supporting Road Asset Management in the road sector. It also contributed to Focus Area 3, particularly Objective 3.2: Putting in place enhanced disaster risk management and climate and disaster resilience, by integrating climate-resilient design into road rehabilitation, consistent with the CPF’s emphasis on disaster and climate resilience.

It also contributed to the Eighth National Socio-Economic Development Plan (2016– 2020) and Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 9 (resilient infrastructure) and 13 (climate action). B. The project made major contributions to building institutional capacity within the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MPWT), especially in contract management, safeguards compliance, performance-based road maintenance, and life-cycle asset management. Road safety emerged as a critical concern during implementation. Several traffic collisions occurred, including fatalities in 2020, 2021, and 2022, prompting detailed Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and the development of Safeguards Corrective Action Plans (SCAP). These investigations revealed contributing factors such as poor road conditions, inadequate signage, insufficient lighting, and driver negligence. In response, the project implemented a range of safety measures including improved signage, lighting, and road maintenance. A dedicated Road Safety Engineer was assigned, and traffic management plans were incorporated into the ESMP and monitored monthly by the supervision consultant. Fiduciary Compliance 79. Financial Management (FM) and procurement arrangements were implemented in accordance with World Bank guidelines. The project maintained adequate financial records, submitted timely interim unaudited financial reports (IUFRs), and received unqualified audit opinions throughout the implementation period. Procurement was carried out using World Bank procedures, and the OPBRC was competitively tendered. While the project experienced some delays in contract execution due to market volatility and currency depreciation, these were managed through contract amendments and close supervision. The fiduciary performance of the project was rated Satisfactory. C. BANK PERFORMANCE Quality at Entry 80. The World Bank’s performance during preparation was highly satisfactory.

Recognizing impediments to the proposed toll road, the World Bank supported MPWT to identify an alternative project design that strategically aligned with Lao PDR’s priorities and the World Bank’s engagement objectives. While focusing on improving road condition, safety, and climate resilience along a critical national corridor, the project design indirectly facilitated long-term institutional development priorities related to maintenance. Introducing the OPBRC—the first of its kind in Lao PDR— reflected a forward-looking and innovative approach to road asset management. The World Bank used its convening power effectively to bring together multiple financiers—AIIB and NDF—under a coordinated framework, leveraging complementary expertise and financing. This was the first project in the EAP transport portfolio to mobilize co-financing from AIIB. 81. The project design was technically robust, incorporating climate adaptation measures such as raised road profiles and high-capacity drainage systems. A World Bank comparison of lifecycle costs identified PCC as the most costeffective pavement option. Environmental and social safeguards were integrated early, with a Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) and a functioning GRM in place.

The project also embedded gender-sensitive design elements, including improved Official Use Only Page 13 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT pedestrian facilities near markets and schools, and achieved 35 percent female employment target under OPBRC implementation. Fiduciary and procurement arrangements were sound, and the results framework was realistic, practical, and measurable. Implementation arrangements were embedded within existing institutional structures, and risks were appropriately identified and mitigated. While the complexity of the OPBRC model and the land titling process required sustained attention during implementation, these were well anticipated and addressed through early design and institutional engagement. Rating: Highly Satisfactory. Quality of Supervision 82. The World Bank’s supervision of the NR13 project was proactive, consistent, and technically strong. The World Bank maintained close engagement with the client and development partners throughout implementation, conducting regular implementation support missions, bi-weekly technical meetings, and field visits. Coordination with co-financiers — AIIB and NDF — through joint missions was a notable strength which enabled streamlined and harmonized support to the Government, reduced transaction costs for the implementing agencies, and ensured consistent messaging and alignment across development partners.

Performance reporting was candid and action-oriented, and the World Bank’s engagement contributed significantly to the project’s timely completion and achievement of its development outcomes. 83. The project’s turnaround from a Substantial-risk operation to a strong performer was driven by consistent leadership and the presence of the World Bank’s Country Office. Their contextual knowledge, language fluency, and longterm engagement enabled agile responses to evolving challenges, including procurement delays, safeguard complexities, and external shocks such as COVID-19 and flooding. This continuity proved essential for maintaining momentum and ensuring effective coordination across central and provincial levels. 84. Strategic use of restructurings and support to the OPBRC model significantly expanded the project’s impact. The inclusion of an additional 6 km of road improvements and full utilization of project savings increased the project’s economic benefits (see paragraph 47). The World Bank played a key role in enhancing the quality of OPBRC bid documents by mobilizing an international expert. World Bank support for the Sustainability Plan and Maintenance Plan and overall institutionalization of OPBRC has contributed to sustainability (see paragraphs 52 and 87). Rating: Highly Satisfactory Justification of Overall Rating of Bank Performance 85. The World Bank’s overall performance is rated Highly Satisfactory.

Preparation was highly satisfactory, with strong strategic alignment, sound technical design, and effective integration of safeguards, fiduciary, and institutional arrangements. Supervision was proactive and well-coordinated with co-financiers. RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME 86. Institutional capacity strengthening and sector dialogue provided strong support to sustainability. MPWT has established the capacity to independently implement the remainder of the ongoing seven-year maintenance phase (see paragraph 52). The success of the OPBRC demonstration, presented to the National Assembly, has contributed to scaling up to ten ongoing OPBRC contracts. In parallel, MPWT has stepped-up efforts to generate funding through user charges, including an initial focus on tolling truck traffic on NR13 South which may expand to NR13 North. A new axel load control station is planned on NR13 North in addition to reactivation of the existing station. 87. Despite these efforts, the ability to fully fund road network maintenance remains challenged by limited resources and high emergency repair costs, which pose a moderate risk to the sustainability of project outcomes. The recent Lao Road Sector Financing ASA revealed that, over the past four years, average annual road network investment was Official Use Only Page 14 The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT US$152.5 million, including most Development Partner contributions for the road sector.

This amount is less than half of the optimal funding required to meet network needs over the next five years. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 88. A simple and flexible project design and scalable PDO and indicators facilitated implementation and responsiveness to evolving development needs. The project design consisting of a few key contracts reduced transaction costs and enabled the client to focus resources and attention adapting to the OPBRC contract format and addressing other implementation challenges. Easing into the OPBRC approach was particularly important given capacity constraints within the country context. The PDO and outcome indicators were simple and readily scalable, allowing for adjustments to mitigate risks such as potential cost escalations, as well as to capitalize on opportunities like scale-up restructuring. 89. Strong client commitment, hands-on support, proactive training, strategic market engagement, and robust technical support were critical to the successful roll-out of OPBRC contracting. Implementing Agency ownership of the demonstration OPBRC at the Ministerial level was a critical factor contributing to rapid institutionalization through training, acquisition of monitoring equipment, and establishment of a monitoring unit.

Timely market outreach and training of contractors increased their understanding of the OPBRC model and collected feedback on key contract parameters – such as the proportion of contract costs to be paid during the maintenance period – leading to a stronger market response. The World Bank’s support to mobilizing an international performance-based contracting expert contributed to the high quality of OPBRC bidding documents. These experiences highlighted the need for tailored capacity-building, iterative contract refinement, and sustained technical support. 90. Close Development Partner coordination strengthened the project design, implementation, and impact. Financing and implementation support from IDA, AIIB, and NDF for works, resettlement, and supervision, enabled the project to achieve greater scale and impact, in line with development partner priorities. The project approach to Road safety and Axel Load control was designed and implemented according to ongoing programs supported by IDA, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), and German Development Bank (KfW). Close cooperation between the World Bank, AIIB, and NDF provided strong implementation support to the Implementing Agency, MPWT. The alignment of financing and technical support demonstrated that coordinated development finance can amplify impact beyond tangible physical outputs.

The efficiency analysis for the ICR of the project is based on a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) approach, which follows the same methodology at appraisal stage. The efficiency analysis covers the time horizon of 30 years (2018-2047), based on the life cycle of actual sub-projects implemented which are road improvement. The project supported the rehabilitation of 64 km of National Road 13 North.

The key assumptions include: (i) the discount rate of 12 percent; (ii) the Standard Conversion Factor (SCF) of 0.92 for investment and 0.87 for maintenance; (iii) the project could help avoid some of the emergency maintenance due to the climate resiliency improvement; (iv) the speed improvement from 30 km/h to 60 km/h; and, (v) traffic growth of 3 percent (until 2025, and 2 percent afterward). 2. At appraisal, the EIRR was estimated at 26.3%, with a net present value (NPV) of US$121.97 million. The ex-post analysis conducted 2025 for the 58 km Sikeut–Phonhong and 6 km Sikhai–Sikeut sections revealed significantly stronger performance with an overall EIRR at 38.5% and NPV of US$180 million. 3. Key economic benefits are from lower vehicle operating costs (VOC) due to the improved road conditions, reduced travel time, reduced emergency repair costs, value of time saving for freight delays, and reduced road accidents. The economic internal rate of return (EIRR) at completion is estimated at 38.5% with net present value (NPV) of US$180 million. The project’s EIRR is higher than the level envisioned at appraisal due to the lower actual investment cost and the additional 6 km of road improvement (with high traffic volume). This provides larger benefits from VOC and VOT savings, and that the economic analysis at appraisal was more conservative with some of the improvement assumptions. Figure A4.1 shows the share of the economic benefits.

The majority of the economic benefits are from the reduction of VOT (50%) and VOC (44%). Figure 4A.1: Share of the economic benefits Freight Travel Time Savings (VOD) 2% Road Accidents 2% Economic EM cost avoided 2% VOC Savings 44% Pax Travel Time Saving (VOT) 50% 4. Competitive procurement generated notable cost savings. Civil works bid prices were approximately 30% lower than the engineer’s cost estimates, resulting in savings of around US$12 million. These savings enabled the inclusion of an additional 6 km of road improvement works (Sikhai–Sikeut section), which was widened from two to four lanes. Despite Page 24 Official Use Only The World Bank Lao National Road 13 Improvement and Maintenance (P163730) ICR DOCUMENT the expanded scope, Component 1 remained below its originally allocated budget. As a result, the EIRR increased from 26% to 39% as the road rehabilitation length increased from 58 km to 64 km. 5. An analysis of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions was undertaken based on fuel consumption rates at different speeds under ‘with project’ and ‘without project’ scenarios. Without the project, the deteriorated condition of the roads would limit vehicle speeds, leading to higher fuel consumption per vehicle-km compared to the ‘with-project’ scenario. The project’s improved road condition leads to more efficient travel speeds, and hence lower fuel consumption. Gross GHG emission in the ‘with project’ scenario is 2,638,753 tCO2e.

Total net GHG emission is estimated to be −447,478tCO2e — a net reduction over the evaluation period (30 years). The annual average net GHG emission is −14,916tCO2e per year. The social benefit from GHG reduction is estimated to be US$34 million, based on social cost of emission reduction from the World Bank’s Guidance Note on Shadow Price of Carbon in Economic Analysis (2024). 6. The project length was extended by 22 months; however, the time extension helped the project be more economically efficient. The extended project duration allowed more time for stakeholder engagement, safeguards resolution, and the inclusion of additional high impact works. The longer time also allowed the project to complete an additional 6 km, which added to the benefits without additional costs to the project. By project close, the full 64 km corridor had been upgraded or rehabilitated, exceeding the scope envisaged at appraisal. The overall efficiency for this project is rated High. The OPBRC model has demonstrated improved efficiency in road development and maintenance, leading MPWT to expand its application to other roads including NR13 South (five contracts), NR2 under SEAREC (five contracts), and additional forthcoming projects. MPWT extends its gratitude to the World Bank, the principal donor, as well as AIIB and NDF for their co-financing and parallel financing respectively contributions to this initiative. The Ministry acknowledges their active support throughout project preparation and implementation, including market sounding, OPBRC training, development of financing structures, standard bidding documentation, service level specifications, procurement processes, and the preparation of safeguard instruments such as the Resettlement Action Plan and ESMP, alongside traffic management plans and close monitoring of contract implementation, safeguard compliance, and RAP execution. These efforts were instrumental in ensuring project success. In addition to financial support, the donors provided valuable guidance that strengthened the capacity of MPWT and the local contracting industry regarding OPBRC preparation and implementation. To promote the long-term sustainability of this OPBRC contract, MPWT has developed a comprehensive sustainability plan.
